newsitem.title: UK: New Bank of England panel reviews interest rates.
newsitem.headline: New Bank of England panel reviews interest rates.

text.p: The Bank of England's new monetary policy committee, empowered by the Labour government to set interest rates, began its first two-day meeting on Thursday amid unprecedented uncertainty over the outcome.
The meeting began at 1400 GMT and was due to resume on Friday morning but the central bank declined to say what time Thusday's session would end.
Financial markets were expecting a quarter-point rise to 6.50 percent in official interest rates when the Bank announces the outcome of the meeting at 1100 GMT on Friday.

But the radical changes made to Britain's monetary framework by the new government, coupled with mixed inflationary signals from economic data, meant few analysts were making forecasts with any confidence.
The Confederation of British Industry said the committee faced a very difficult decision but on balance rates should be left unchanged.

"Interest rates can be left on hold for the moment, firstly because we want to see the budget and secondly because a rise could push the pound still higher," said Sudhir Junankar, associate director of economic analysis.
Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown is set to clarify the bank's inflation target at next week's Mansion House speech and will present his first budget on July 2.
The monetary committee must set policy for an unbalanced economic recovery in which a lively services sector contrasts with sluggish manufacturing output growth.

"The bank is probably itching to raise rates but the next month will bring the budget, news on the inflation target and evidence of the impact the windfall payments are having on consumption. So I think it may decide to hold off until July," said David Philpotts, UK economist at Schroders.

He was referring to windfalls worth up to 30 billion pounds ($49 billion) which millions of Britons will receive this year as mutually owned building societies and insurance companies turn themselves into banks.
Tom Rayner, an economist at Societe Generale, said he thought the central bank might wait, even though it warned several weeks ago that rates would have to rise further.
"The risks of waiting a month don't seem that great to me," Rayner said. "It is finely balanced but we think they will probably wait."
A Reuters poll of 21 economists showed a narrow majority anticipated a rate increase, with 12 expecting base rates to rise to 6.5 percent from the present 6.25 percent.
Bank Governor Eddie George said on Wednesday that the exchange rate would be the key focus at the meeting.

"The immediate problem is to balance the degree of tension between the pressure of domestic demand, which has been running a bit above a sustainable rate, with the exaggerated strength of the exchange rate," he told reporters in Switzerland.
Britain's manufacturing sector has been ravaged by the pound's recent strength -- up almost 20 percent on a trade-weighted basis since last August -- and is growing only slowly.
Meanwhile, the bigger services sector, insulated from the exchange rate by its largely domestic customer base, is booming.
A rate rise on Friday could send the pound even higher, hitting the weakest part of the economy hardest. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
